library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

# Import the data
cases.2 <- read_tsv("cases-2.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)
population.2 <- read_tsv("population-2.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Define the order of the age groups
age_order <- c(
  "0-4", "5-9", "10-14", "15-19", "20-24", "25-29",
  "30-34", "35-39", "40-44", "45-49", "50-54", "55-59",
  "60-64", "65-69", "70-74", "75-79", "80-84", "85-89"
)

# Define sex categories and colours
sexes <- c("Female", "Male")
cols <- c(Female = "#B34D70", Male = "#227C9D")
```

# Introduction

This assignment analyses colon cancer cases in Sweden from 1970
to 2022 by calendar year, age group and sex. The supplied data
cover people aged 0–89 years.

# Question 1: Cases by age group and sex

The merged dataset, called `cases`, contains five-year age groups,
sex, calendar year, the number of incident cases (`n`) and the
population size (`n_pop`). Each row represents an age-year-sex
combination.

We sum the cases across calendar years within each age group
and sex to compare their distributions over the study period.

```{r q1-aggregate, echo=TRUE}
cases <- left_join(cases.2, population.2,
                   by = c("agegroup", "sex", "year"))
cases$agegroup <- factor(cases$agegroup, levels = age_order)
by_age <- aggregate(n ~ agegroup + sex, cases, sum)
```

```{r q1-prepare, include=FALSE}
by_age$agegroup <- factor(by_age$agegroup, levels = age_order)
```

```{r q1-plot, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Colon cancer cases pooled over 1970–2022, by age group and sex."}
ggplot(by_age, aes(x = agegroup, y = n, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of cases by age group and sex",
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Cases"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

**Interpretation.** Case counts generally increase with age,
reaching a peak at ages 75–79 for both sexes before decreasing
in the oldest age groups. This decrease does not necessarily
indicate a lower incidence rate, because population sizes
differ across age groups.

# Question 2: Annual cases by sex

We sum the cases across age groups, retaining one total
for each calendar year and sex.

```{r q2-aggregate, echo=TRUE}
annual_cases <- aggregate(n ~ year + sex, cases, sum)
```

```{r q2-plot, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Annual colon cancer cases, ages 0–89, separately by sex."}
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

for (s in sexes) {
  a <- annual_cases[annual_cases$sex == s, ]
  a <- a[order(a$year), ]

  plot(
    a$year, a$n,
    type = "l",
    col = cols[s],
    main = s,
    xlab = "Year",
    ylab = "Annual cases",
    ylim = range(annual_cases$n)
  )
}

par(old_par)
```

**Interpretation.** The figure shows an increase in recorded
cases in both sexes. Female counts rise from 1,196 in 1970
to 2,713 in 2022, while male counts rise from 1,093 to 2,713.
These counts do not distinguish between changes in population
size, age composition and incidence.

\newpage

# Question 3: Population size by age, year and sex

The second dataset, called `population.2`, is structured similarly
to the cases dataset, with a column named `n_pop` for population size.

We created plots covering all calendar years, comparing females
and males using coloured lines. Population labels are shown
in thousands.

```{r q3-prepare, echo=TRUE}
population_plot <- population.2 %>%
  mutate(agegroup = factor(agegroup, levels = age_order))
```

```{r q3-plot, fig.cap="Population size over all years from 1970 to 2022.", fig.height=6.2, fig.width=7, out.width="90%"}
ggplot(
  population_plot,
  aes(x = year, y = n_pop, colour = sex)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ agegroup, ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1970, 1990, 2010, 2022)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = function(x) x / 1000
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Population size over time by age group and sex",
    x = "Calendar year",
    y = "Population (thousands)",
    colour = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

**Interpretation.** Population size changes over time, and these
changes differ across age groups. The share aged 65–89 increases
from approximately 15.3% to 21.9% among females and from 12.3%
to 19.0% among males. Therefore, both the female and male
populations become older. This matters because age composition
influences the crude incidence rate.

# Question 7: Poisson regression for the total number of cases

We first create the data frame with the total number of cases and the total
population size in each calendar year and sex (summing over all age groups).
Calendar year is centred at 1970, so that the intercept of the model
corresponds to the rate in 1970.

```{r q7-data, echo=TRUE}
# Total cases and total population per calendar year and sex
total_data <- cases %>%
  group_by(year, sex) %>%
  summarise(
    n = sum(n, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_pop = sum(n_pop, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Observed crude rate per 100,000 person-years (used in Questions 8-9)
total_data$rate100k <- 100000 * total_data$n / total_data$n_pop

# Calendar year centred at 1970; Male is the reference category
total_data$year0 <- total_data$year - 1970
total_data$sex <- factor(total_data$sex, levels = c("Male", "Female"))

# Sanity check: 53 years x 2 sexes, no missing values
stopifnot(nrow(total_data) == 106, !anyNA(total_data))
```

Let $Y_{ts}$ be the number of cases in year $t$ and sex $s$, and $P_{ts}$ the
population size. The model is

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y_{ts}) = \mu_{ts}, \qquad
\log(\mu_{ts}) = \log(P_{ts}) + \beta_0 + \beta_1 (\text{year}_t - 1970) + \beta_2 \text{Female}_s ,
\qquad \text{Var}(Y_{ts}) = \phi\,\mu_{ts},
$$

so that $\log(P_{ts})$ is an offset and the model describes the log incidence
rate $\log(\mu_{ts}/P_{ts})$. The mean model is the Poisson model; the
dispersion parameter $\phi$ is estimated from the data (quasi-Poisson), see
the check below. For $\phi = 1$ this is the ordinary Poisson model.

First we fit the ordinary Poisson model and check the Poisson variance
assumption.

```{r q7-poisson, echo=TRUE}
# Ordinary Poisson model (used for the dispersion check)
m_pois <- glm(
  n ~ year0 + sex + offset(log(n_pop)),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = total_data
)

# Overdispersion: Pearson chi-square / residual degrees of freedom (close to 1 if OK)
disp_pois <- sum(residuals(m_pois, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m_pois)
disp_pois
```

The dispersion is `r round(disp_pois, 2)`, clearly larger than 1, so the
counts vary more around the fitted model than a Poisson distribution allows
(overdispersion). The Poisson standard errors would be too small and the
confidence intervals too narrow. The point estimates are not affected. We
therefore use a quasi-Poisson model, which gives the same estimates but
multiplies the standard errors by $\sqrt{\hat\phi}$. Note that part of this
overdispersion may be lack of fit of the linear year trend rather than purely
random year-to-year variation (see the check below).

```{r q7-model, echo=TRUE}
# Final model: quasi-Poisson, offset = log(population), year (linear) + sex
m_total <- glm(
  n ~ year0 + sex + offset(log(n_pop)),
  family = quasipoisson(link = "log"),
  data = total_data
)
summary(m_total)

# Rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals (t-distribution, since phi is estimated)
est   <- coef(m_total)
se    <- sqrt(diag(vcov(m_total)))
tcrit <- qt(0.975, df.residual(m_total))
rr_total <- exp(cbind(RR = est, lower = est - tcrit * se, upper = est + tcrit * se))
round(rr_total, 4)
```

To motivate the choice of how year and sex are modelled, we compare the final
model with two more flexible alternatives: a natural spline for calendar year
(non-linear trend) and a year-by-sex interaction (different yearly change for
males and females). The models are compared with F-tests, which account for
the overdispersion (AIC is not defined for quasi-Poisson models; the AIC of
the corresponding Poisson models is shown for reference only).

```{r q7-check, echo=TRUE}
library(splines)
m_total_spline <- glm(n ~ ns(year0, df = 3) + sex + offset(log(n_pop)),
                      family = quasipoisson, data = total_data)  # non-linear year
m_total_int <- glm(n ~ year0 * sex + offset(log(n_pop)),
                   family = quasipoisson, data = total_data)     # year-by-sex interaction

# F-tests against the final model
a_spline <- anova(m_total, m_total_spline, test = "F")
a_int    <- anova(m_total, m_total_int,    test = "F")
a_spline
a_int

# Poisson versions of the alternative models (AIC for reference only)
m_pois_spline <- update(m_pois, . ~ ns(year0, df = 3) + sex + offset(log(n_pop)))
m_pois_int    <- update(m_pois, . ~ year0 * sex + offset(log(n_pop)))
AIC(m_pois, m_pois_spline, m_pois_int)

# Dispersion (Pearson) of the three models
sapply(list(linear = m_pois, spline = m_pois_spline, interaction = m_pois_int),
       function(m) sum(residuals(m, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m))
```

```{r q7-values, include=FALSE}
p_spline <- a_spline$`Pr(>F)`[2]
p_int    <- a_int$`Pr(>F)`[2]
b_int    <- coef(m_total_int)
rr_year_male   <- exp(b_int["year0"])
rr_year_female <- exp(b_int["year0"] + b_int["year0:sexFemale"])

disp_spline <- sum(residuals(m_pois_spline, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m_pois_spline)
# Largest relative difference between fitted rates of the spline and linear models
max_diff_spline <- 100 * max(abs(fitted(m_total_spline) / fitted(m_total) - 1))
```

**Motivation.**

* **Offset.** The number of cases depends on the size of the population, so
  we model rates instead of counts. Including $\log(\text{population})$ as an
  offset (coefficient fixed to 1) does this, and the exponentiated
  coefficients are rate ratios.
* **Distribution.** The dispersion is `r round(disp_pois, 2)` (> 1), so the
  Poisson assumption $\text{Var}(Y) = \mu$ does not hold. We use a
  quasi-Poisson model, which corrects the standard errors and confidence
  intervals for the overdispersion. Part of the overdispersion reflects lack
  of fit of the linear trend: it falls to `r round(disp_spline, 2)` when a
  non-linear year term is allowed.
* **Calendar year.** Year is included as a continuous, linear term on the log
  scale. This gives a smooth curve and a single, easily interpreted rate ratio
  per year, which suits the aim of smoothing the random variation between
  years. The F-test for a natural spline gives
  p = `r format.pval(p_spline, digits = 2)`, so the data
  `r ifelse(p_spline < 0.05, "show evidence of a non-linear trend", "give no clear evidence against a log-linear trend")`.
  We nevertheless keep the linear term as a deliberate simplification: the
  fitted rates of the spline model differ from those of the linear model by at
  most `r round(max_diff_spline, 1)`%, which is small compared with the
  overall increase, and the linear model gives one average yearly rate ratio.
  Part of the non-linearity is probably due to the changing age structure,
  which is handled in Questions 10-13. The spline fit is shown in Figure 5 as
  a sensitivity analysis.
* **Sex.** Sex is included as a binary factor (male as reference) with a main
  effect only, i.e. a constant female/male rate ratio. The F-test for a
  year-by-sex interaction gives p = `r format.pval(p_int, digits = 2)`;
  the estimated yearly rate ratio is `r round(rr_year_male, 4)` for males and
  `r round(rr_year_female, 4)` for females. The difference in yearly change is
  therefore small in practice, and we keep the main-effect model to obtain
  one rate ratio for sex. The limitation is stated in the assumptions in
  Question 8.

# Question 8: Estimated incidence rates in 1970 and 2020

```{r q8-pred, echo=TRUE}
# Predicted rates per 100,000 person-years (population set to 100,000)
newdata_q8 <- expand.grid(
  year = c(1970, 2020),
  sex = factor(c("Male", "Female"), levels = c("Male", "Female")),
  n_pop = 100000
)
newdata_q8$year0 <- newdata_q8$year - 1970

# For a quasi-Poisson model, se.fit is already scaled by sqrt(dispersion)
pred_q8 <- predict(m_total, newdata = newdata_q8, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
newdata_q8$rate100k <- exp(pred_q8$fit)
newdata_q8$lower    <- exp(pred_q8$fit - tcrit * pred_q8$se.fit)
newdata_q8$upper    <- exp(pred_q8$fit + tcrit * pred_q8$se.fit)

res_q8 <- newdata_q8[order(newdata_q8$year, newdata_q8$sex),
                     c("year", "sex", "rate100k", "lower", "upper")]
knitr::kable(res_q8, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Year", "Sex", "Rate per 100,000", "Lower 95% CI", "Upper 95% CI"))

# The same rates calculated directly from the coefficients
b <- unname(coef(m_total))   # (Intercept), year0, sexFemale
rates_by_hand <- c(
  Male_1970   = 1e5 * exp(b[1]),
  Female_1970 = 1e5 * exp(b[1] + b[3]),
  Male_2020   = 1e5 * exp(b[1] + 50 * b[2]),
  Female_2020 = 1e5 * exp(b[1] + 50 * b[2] + b[3])
)
round(rates_by_hand, 1)
```

```{r q8-values, include=FALSE}
# Values used in the text below
r <- setNames(res_q8$rate100k, paste(res_q8$sex, res_q8$year, sep = "_"))
rr_year  <- exp(b[2])
rr_sex   <- exp(b[3])
```

**Interpretation.** According to the model, the incidence rate in 1970 was
`r round(r["Male_1970"], 1)` per 100,000 person-years among males and
`r round(r["Female_1970"], 1)` among females. In 2020 the estimated rates were
`r round(r["Male_2020"], 1)` among males and `r round(r["Female_2020"], 1)`
among females. The estimated rate ratio per calendar year is
`r round(rr_year, 4)` (`r round(100 * (rr_year - 1), 2)`% per year,
`r round(100 * (exp(10 * b[2]) - 1), 1)`% per 10 years), which corresponds to
an increase of `r round(100 * (exp(50 * b[2]) - 1), 0)`% between 1970 and 2020.
The rate ratio for females compared with males is `r round(rr_sex, 3)`.
The confidence intervals are based on the quasi-Poisson model and are therefore
wider than those from an ordinary Poisson model. They describe the uncertainty
of the fitted rates given that the model is correct; they do not include
uncertainty from the model specification (linear trend, constant sex ratio).

**Assumptions.**

1. The log incidence rate changes linearly with calendar year, i.e. the rate
   changes by the same constant percentage every year (exponential change).
   The F-test in Question 7 showed
   `r ifelse(p_spline < 0.05, "some evidence against this", "no clear evidence against this")`,
   so it is an approximation.
2. The change per year is the same for males and females (no interaction),
   and the female/male rate ratio is the same in every calendar year. The
   absolute difference between the sexes can still differ between years, since
   the difference is constant only on the multiplicative scale. The
   interaction test in Question 7 (p = `r format.pval(p_int, digits = 2)`)
   suggests that the yearly increase is slightly smaller among females, so the
   sex difference is not exactly constant over time.
3. The variance of the number of cases is proportional to its mean,
   $\text{Var}(Y) = \phi\mu$, with $\phi$ estimated from the data
   (overdispersion relative to Poisson), the numbers of cases in different
   years and sexes are independent given the population size, and the
   population on July 1st approximates the person-years at risk.
4. The model uses crude rates over ages 0-89 and does not adjust for the age
   distribution (this is done in Question 10).

# Question 9: Estimated incidence rates over calendar year by sex

```{r q9-data, echo=TRUE}
# Model-based rates for every calendar year, per 100,000 person-years
grid_q9 <- expand.grid(
  year = 1970:2022,
  sex = factor(c("Male", "Female"), levels = c("Male", "Female")),
  n_pop = 100000
)
grid_q9$year0 <- grid_q9$year - 1970

pred_q9 <- predict(m_total, newdata = grid_q9, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
grid_q9$rate100k <- exp(pred_q9$fit)
grid_q9$lower    <- exp(pred_q9$fit - tcrit * pred_q9$se.fit)
grid_q9$upper    <- exp(pred_q9$fit + tcrit * pred_q9$se.fit)

# Sensitivity: non-linear (spline) year effect, same sex effect
pred_q9s <- predict(m_total_spline, newdata = grid_q9, type = "link")
grid_q9$rate_spline <- exp(pred_q9s)
```

```{r q9-plot, echo=TRUE, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Model-based incidence rates (solid lines, with 95% confidence intervals from the quasi-Poisson model) and observed crude rates (points) by calendar year and sex. Dashed lines are loess smoothers of the observed rates."}
ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = grid_q9,
    aes(x = year, ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = sex),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_q9,
    aes(x = year, y = rate100k, colour = sex),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = total_data,
    aes(x = year, y = rate100k, colour = sex),
    size = 1, alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    data = total_data,
    aes(x = year, y = rate100k, colour = sex),
    method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols) +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated incidence rate of colon cancer by calendar year",
    x = "Calendar year",
    y = "Rate per 100,000 person-years",
    colour = "Sex",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r q9-plot2, echo=TRUE, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Sensitivity analysis on the log scale: final log-linear model (solid), model with a natural spline for calendar year (dotted), and loess smoothers of the observed rates (dashed)."}
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = total_data,
    aes(x = year, y = rate100k, colour = sex),
    size = 1, alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_q9,
    aes(x = year, y = rate100k, colour = sex),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_q9,
    aes(x = year, y = rate_spline, colour = sex),
    linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    data = total_data,
    aes(x = year, y = rate100k, colour = sex),
    method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols) +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated incidence rate (log scale)",
    x = "Calendar year",
    y = "Rate per 100,000 person-years (log scale)",
    colour = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The table below shows how far the observed crude rates lie from the fitted
model (ratio observed / fitted, averaged within each period). A ratio above 1
means that the model underestimates the observed rate.

```{r q9-values, echo=TRUE}
# Observed crude rate relative to the fitted model, by period
total_data$fit_rate <- 100000 * fitted(m_total) / total_data$n_pop
total_data$ratio <- total_data$rate100k / total_data$fit_rate
total_data$period <- cut(total_data$year, c(1969, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2022),
                         labels = c("1970-80", "1981-90", "1991-2000", "2001-10", "2011-22"))
ratio_tab <- round(tapply(total_data$ratio, list(total_data$period, total_data$sex), mean), 3)
knitr::kable(ratio_tab, caption = "Mean ratio of observed to fitted rate by period and sex.")
```

**Interpretation.**

* **Overall pattern.** The estimated incidence rate of colon cancer increases
  steadily in both sexes, from about `r round(r["Male_1970"], 0)`-`r round(r["Female_1970"], 0)`
  per 100,000 person-years in 1970 to about `r round(r["Male_2020"], 0)`-`r round(r["Female_2020"], 0)`
  in 2020 (an increase of about `r round(100 * (exp(50 * b[2]) - 1), 0)`%).
  The rate is somewhat higher among females throughout, by about
  `r round(100 * (rr_sex - 1), 1)`% in the model.
* **Model versus observed.** The model curves remove the random variation
  between years seen in the observed rates (points). The confidence bands are
  wider than they would be under an ordinary Poisson model, because the
  observed rates vary around the fitted line more than Poisson variation
  allows (dispersion `r round(disp_pois, 2)`, partly due to the departures
  from a straight line described below).
* **Fit of the assumptions.** The loess smoothers follow the model lines
  fairly closely, so a log-linear trend is a reasonable summary. There are
  systematic departures, however (see the table above): the observed female
  rates are above the model line in 1981-90 (on average
  `r ratio_tab["1981-90", "Female"]` times the fitted rate) and below it after
  2000 (`r ratio_tab["2001-10", "Female"]` in 2001-10 and
  `r ratio_tab["2011-22", "Female"]` in 2011-22), while the male rates are
  below the model line in the 1970s (`r ratio_tab["1970-80", "Male"]`) and
  above it in 2011-22 (`r ratio_tab["2011-22", "Male"]`). As a result the
  observed rates of the two sexes move closer to each other over time, whereas
  the model keeps a constant ratio. This agrees with the interaction test in
  Question 7. The spline model in Figure 5 follows the loess curves a little
  better, but the differences from the log-linear model are small compared
  with the overall increase.
* **Caveat.** The rates are crude (not age-adjusted). Part of the increase,
  and part of the departures from a straight line, can be due to the ageing of
  the population (Figure 3), which is addressed in Questions 10-13.
